extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers, and practitioners of scientific method and inductive logic (scientists, experimentalists, philosophers of science)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and criteria for using and evaluating the four inductive methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Joint/Indirect Difference), and for handling plural causes and compound effects in scientific investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: When varied instances that produce the same effect agree only in containing antecedent A, that fact suggests A is connected with the effect; repetition and variation strengthen the presumption in favor of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small numbers of agreeing instances (e.g., only two) are of little value because the same effect may arise from different causes (plurality of causes). The method yields at best a slight probability unless instances are indefinitely multiplied and varied. Use it as suggestion that must be tested further (preferably by Method of Difference or deductive reasoning). Example: planetary paths and refracted rays were ascertained by direct measurement / agreement; but agreement should lead to difference-experiments for proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: If two instances differ only by the presence of antecedent A, and the effect appears in the former but not the latter, then A is either the cause of the effect or an indispensable part of its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method is free from the characteristic imperfection of the Method of Agreement arising from plurality of causes; two instances (one positive, one negative) suffice for a complete and rigorous induction in the case considered. Recommended as the primary direct test to ascertain causation when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method of Agreement and Difference (Indirect Method of Difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine affirmative and negative premises: instances with the phenomenon present agree only in A, and instances where it is absent agree only in not-A; under these conditions, A must be the only possible cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This joint/indirect method is, after the Direct Method of Difference, the most powerful inductive instrument, especially in observational sciences where direct experiment is limited (example: cause of dew). The negative premise is especially valuable but often practically difficult because exhausting the field of negation is hard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Negative Instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Negative instances—cases in which a phenomenon does not occur—are particularly informative and can free the Method of Agreement from its characteristic imperfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although theoretically powerful, negative-instance analysis is generally difficult because it's harder to enumerate and exhaust non-occurrences (e.g., determining what all non-transparent substances have in common is infeasible). Thus negative instances are best used in conjunction with positive instances and difference-method reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plurality of Causes (multiple sufficient causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A single observed effect may be producible by several independent causes; the same phenomenon can follow from different antecedents in different instances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plurality undermines the Method of Agreement unless many varied instances exclude the possibility of different causes. Detect plurality either by separate sets of instances showing different causes, or by failing to find any common antecedent among all instances. When plurality cannot be excluded, treat distinct antecedents provisionally as separate sufficient causes. Assessing how many instances suffice to rebut plurality belongs to the Theory of Probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture (Composition) of Effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes act concurrently their separate effects may be compounded, partly cancel one another, or merge into a sum, so that the separate contributions are disguised and not directly discernible by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This composition of causes greatly complicates direct inductive investigation: the four direct methods are largely unequal to disentangling such mixtures. Deduction (theoretical analysis) is usually required to unravel these complexities; direct methods mainly supply premises and verification. Examples: concurrent mechanical forces producing resultant motion, or several causes producing a net zero (equilibrium).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation vs. Composition (heteropathic effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish cases where combining causes produces entirely new phenomena (transformation, e.g., chemical compounds) from those where separate effects persist and simply combine (composition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transformation (heteropathic effects that can be decomposed, e.g., water ↔ hydrogen + oxygen) is amenable to experimental analysis because the compound can reproduce its components; chemical analysis exploits this. Composition (e.g., intermingled forces or blended sensations) resists such analysis because the individual factors often cannot be reproduced from the compound, requiring synthetic study of components and deduction about their combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express causal laws as tendencies, not absolute results
rubrics_metrics.description: Because causes may be counteracted by other concurrent causes, laws of causation should be stated as tendencies (e.g., 'tends to move') rather than assertions of inevitable actual results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stating laws as tendencies avoids the false impression of exceptions; what appear as exceptions are often the action of other concurrent laws. Use terminology that recognizes tendencies (e.g., 'pressure' in mechanics) so that laws remain true without awkward exceptions. This avoids mislabeling concurrent principles as 'exceptions.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overvaluing mere number of instances
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere mass of similar observations adds little evidence unless the added instances exclude further antecedents; repetition of the same kind of instance without novel eliminations is largely useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single instance that eliminates a previously unexcluded antecedent is more valuable than many redundant instances. Repeat identical experiments only to ensure no factual error; otherwise vary circumstances to test and exclude alternative causes. Use variation to strengthen inference against plurality of causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of Deduction in complex causal problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When causes intermix or interfere, deduction (theoretical reasoning) is often necessary to untangle and interpret the observed joint results; the four inductive methods mainly provide premises and verification for such deductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limits of direct experimental/observational methods in compound cases; construct deductive explanations that can be tested by targeted experiments (e.g., those suggested by the Method of Difference) or by comparing with already-established laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental discovery vs. serendipity and systematic combination
rubrics_metrics.description: Some causes of certain effects (especially in transformation cases) are discovered either accidentally, by chance experiments, or gradually through systematic experimentation on combinations of agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where reproduction of causes from effects is possible (chemical analysis), experiment can reveal causes; otherwise serendipity or broad systematic combination experiments are needed. Awareness of reproducibility (e.g., water producing hydrogen and oxygen under analysis) makes experimental search feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of apparent exceptions as concurrent laws
rubrics_metrics.description: What looks like an exception to a law is generally another concurrent principle acting in conjunction with the first, not a true exception to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not categorize an effect as an exception; instead identify the concurrent disturbing force and treat both as comprehensive rules applying across cases (example: atmospheric resistance modifying falling). Proper nomenclature and arrangement should place both principles as concurrent causes, not as law+exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concomitant Variations (as part of inductive toolkit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing how variations in one antecedent accompany variations in the effect helps establish empirical laws (the Method of Concomitant Variations played a large part historically in establishing empirical laws).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concomitant variations to detect relations where direct agreement/difference instances are impractical, but treat such findings as part of the larger inductive/deductive process and seek further verification.
